comment: xfail registry for the full_api_ext table. Same rules as known.json: an
entry that starts passing is reported as xpass and FAILS the run, so the
registry has to be updated when a fix lands.
Everything here was measured against test_fullapi_ext_rust. Note that the
Rust dispatch validates by LIDL TYPE even where the Rust binding is untyped
(`[bstr]` binds as serde_json::Value but is still checked against
Ty::Arr(Ty::Bstr)) — that is what turns E2 into a precise error with a path
instead of a silently wrong value.

xfail.summary: a bstr nested in a container is UTF-8 mangled (bytes >= 0x80 become U+FFFD)

measured.echoBlob payload 00 80 ff: comes back {"_bytes":"AO-_ve-_vQ"} = 00 EF BF BD EF BF BD — each byte >= 0x80 replaced by U+FFFD and re-encoded as UTF-8
measured.echoBytesList([<hi>, <ff>]): ["hi", "\ufffd"] — the tag is gone, the values are strings
measured.echoBlobMap({k: Blob}): the record's payload field becomes the string "hi"
measured.C++ provider, any bstr at depth: dispatch_failed: expected bytes at arg0.payload, got string — the generated codec REFUSES the mangled value instead of accepting it, so the same defect is loud on C++ and silent on Rust

note: The same defect as known.json M5, reached through the ext contract. A
top-level bstr is exact on every provider; the loss is nesting-specific.
This is precisely what the canonical {"_bytes": ...} tag was introduced
to prevent (logos-protocol #21/#23) — defeated one level down.
The corruption is INBOUND, before the module: echoBlob decodes the field
into Vec<u8> and re-encodes it with the same tagged encoder the scalar
path uses, and returned SIX bytes for a three-byte input — i.e. it

The two providers therefore DISAGREE on these cells, and that disagreement is a consequence of E1, not a separate defect: the C++ codec type-checks the byte field and rejects a string, while the Rust side takes [bstr] untyped (serde_json::Value) and passes the corruption through. Fixing E1 makes both green; until then the C++ behaviour is the better one.
xfail.fix_is: a wire-representation question, like M1/M5 — deliberately not guessed at here

xfail.summary: an EMPTY bstr nested in a container arrives as null and fails the call

measured.echoBlob(payload = <empty>): dispatch_failed: expected bytes at arg0.payload, got null
measured.echoBlobList([ok, <empty payload>]): dispatch_failed: expected bytes at arg0[1].payload, got null
measured.echoBytesList([<empty>]): dispatch_failed: expected bytes at arg0[0], got null
measured.echoBytesList([<hi>]): ['hi'] — a NON-empty element gets through (mangled per E1, but through)
measured.echoBytes(<empty>) at top level: b'' — exact, so this is nesting-specific too

note: Distinct from E1: the empty value is DROPPED rather than corrupted, so
the call fails outright instead of returning something wrong. Arguably
the better failure mode of the two — it is at least loud.
The error path is exact (`arg0[1].payload`), which is the record
xfail.fix_is: same family as E1; an empty byte string must survive as an empty byte string, not become null

xfail.summary: known.json M1 seen through a record field

measured.echoBlob(n = 2^64-1): dispatch_failed: expected integer at arg0.n, got number

note: A uint64 above int64max degrades to a double once nested (M1); the
record's typed validation then correctly refuses a float for a `uint`
field. The diagnostic names the exact field path, which is worth pinning
on its own — it is the behaviour that makes a record decode debuggable.
